title: Energy, work, power, and SI dimensions
concept: Energy is a conserved physical quantity that can change form; power is its rate of transfer. Distinguishing these concepts is essential for preserving correct engineering knowledge. A 1 kW device operating for one hour transfers 1 kWh, or exactly 3.6 MJ, but it is not producing 1 kWh at every instant. Work from a force requires displacement in the force direction. A joule is a newton metre, a watt is a joule per second, and electric quantities introduce volts, amperes and ohms. A useful report states the measurement boundary, sign convention, interval, uncertainties and whether values are rated, sampled, inferred or calibrated. Primary units must not be silently mixed with engineering units. Energy per unit mass, area, cycle and delivered service are distinct performance measures.
formula: P=dE/dt; E=∫P dt; 1 Wh=3600 J; 1 kWh=3.6×10^6 J; 1 W=1 kg·m²/s³.
derivation: Dimensional analysis checks equations before computation: power times time has dimensions energy, whereas power divided by time does not. For a time-varying load, multiply average power by the interval only when the average is explicitly measured or defined. Integrating sample values needs an interpolation assumption, not just endpoints. The SI brochure gives the authoritative unit definitions, while sampled energy remains subject to instrument accuracy. A source record can preserve exact unit definitions even when no original laboratory measurements are available.
example: A 600 W heater runs continuously for 30 minutes. Compute 300 Wh = 0.3 kWh = 1.08 MJ by hand and with unit_convert. Repeat for a 600 W peak device whose output varies; explain why its true energy can be lower than the rated calculation.
counterexample: Watts and watt-hours are not interchangeable. Demand charges, power capacity and stored energy answer different questions. An energy value without units and a reference interval is not a physically usable measurement.

title: Conservation boundaries and energy accounting
concept: The first law of thermodynamics is an accounting principle: energy entering, leaving and accumulating inside a chosen system must balance. The boundary can enclose a battery, building, motor, power plant or entire grid. Changes in the boundary move terms between internal transfers and external flows without changing conservation. Real measurements rarely close exactly because sensors have uncertainty, flow channels may be omitted, and stored energy may be difficult to estimate. A nonzero residual identifies an accounting discrepancy; it does not by itself reveal which physical component is faulty. Conservation should be tested against measured input and output with separate uncertainty estimates, not enforced by silently assigning all differences to an arbitrary loss bucket.
formula: ΔE_stored = E_in − E_out, and residual r = E_in − E_out − ΔE_stored.
derivation: The expression comes from integrating conservation over the time interval and classifying each transfer once. Work, heat, chemical fuel, electromagnetic energy and mass-borne enthalpy are different channels but contribute consistently under an explicit system definition. Subtracting inferred storage change from net flow leaves a measurable residual. If a test reports negative residual, possible explanations include unmetered input, inconsistent sign conventions, clock mismatch or drift. Distinguishing those mechanisms requires further observations, not a model’s self-report.
example: A test battery receives 1000 J, delivers 700 J and increases stored energy by 200 J. Its residual is 100 J. Write at least three alternative explanations for the 100 J, identify which additional measurements discriminate between them, and record all quantities as a constructed example.
counterexample: No claim of over-unity may follow from a single nonzero residual. Hidden energy inflow, measurement bias and definition mismatch must be excluded before considering unconventional mechanisms.

title: Thermodynamic state and the first law
concept: Internal energy is a state function: its change depends on initial and final thermodynamic states, not the specific path. Heat and work are process-dependent transfers, not substances stored inside matter. A closed system excludes mass crossing its boundary; open systems require mass-flow enthalpy and kinetic and potential energy terms. The choice of sign convention must be explicit. We use heat into the system as positive and work done by the system as positive. Real engines often cycle through phases where pressure, temperature and composition vary; an ideal gas approximation applies only under conditions for which its constitutive law is adequate. State changes can be represented mathematically but actual thermodynamic properties require reliable material data.
formula: ΔU = Q − W (closed system); W_reversible = ∫P dV; ideal gas PV=nRT.
derivation: The first law integrates energy conservation and assigns heat and work signs. For a reversible isothermal ideal gas, U depends only on T; therefore ΔU=0, so heat received equals the work delivered. Integrating P=nRT/V between V1 and V2 gives W=nRT ln(V2/V1). This result cannot be transferred to irreversible gas expansion against a finite external pressure without modeling the actual process path.
example: Expand one mole of ideal gas reversibly from 0.01 m³ to 0.02 m³ at 300 K. Calculate work by hand using nRT ln 2, then compare with the reversible_ideal_gas_work reference. List how the calculation changes when gas deviates from ideal behavior.
counterexample: A temperature reading does not determine the internal energy of arbitrary material without heat-capacity, phase and composition information. Reversible work is an upper-limit idealization for a given process, not a promise about real devices.

title: Entropy, irreversibility, and the second law
concept: The second law constrains the direction and quality of energy transformations. Energy conservation alone permits many mathematically balanced processes that never occur spontaneously. Entropy quantifies aspects of dispersal and available microscopic arrangements, with reversible heat transfer defining dS=δQ_rev/T. For an isolated system, total entropy cannot decrease. Real engines and electrical conversions create entropy through friction, finite-temperature heat transfer, electrical resistance, mixing and chemical reactions. A useful energy library must distinguish energy from exergy: the latter is the potential to do useful work relative to a reference environment. Two energy quantities of equal joules can have very different capacities for mechanical work.
formula: ΔS_isolated ≥ 0; dS=δQ_rev/T; exergy destroyed = T0 S_generated for a specified reference environment.
derivation: A heat engine that moves heat from a hot source to a cold sink while delivering work can be evaluated by both first- and second-law balances. The inequality arises from the Clausius statement and reversible comparison cycles. Entropy generation identifies quality degradation, even though total joules are conserved. A reversible process maximizes efficiency under the idealized endpoint temperatures, but real material transport imposes finite rates and dissipation.
example: Explain why 1 kWh of electricity and 1 kWh of low-temperature waste heat have equal energy but unequal potential for useful work. Name the ambient reference temperature and which measurements would be needed to quantify exergy.
counterexample: Entropy is not a casual synonym for disorder or the amount of useful knowledge. It does not prove that a computing system cannot improve its performance without external work; accounting must include its environment.

title: Carnot bounds and the meaning of heat-pump COP
concept: A reversible heat engine operating between two fixed thermal reservoirs has a maximum possible thermal efficiency determined only by their absolute temperatures. The corresponding reversed ideal refrigerator and heat pump can move more thermal energy than the mechanical or electrical work they consume, because they transfer ambient heat as well as supply work. Their coefficient of performance can exceed one without violating conservation. This must not be confused with a heat engine that produces more work than heat input. Actual device performance is lower than reversible ideals due to temperature differences needed for finite heat transfer, compressors, throttling, electrical losses and defrost demands.
formula: η_Carnot=1−Tc/Th; COP_heating,max=Th/(Th−Tc); COP_cooling,max=Tc/(Th−Tc), with 0<Tc<Th in kelvin.
derivation: A reversible engine has Qc/Qh=Tc/Th, and useful work Qh−Qc; substituting yields the efficiency. Reversing work and heat flows yields COP expressions. These follow from a reversible-cycle entropy balance, not a particular refrigerant or commercial appliance. Real COP depends on temperatures at the actual heat exchangers, flow rate and part-load operation, not merely outdoor air temperature.
example: For 500 K and 300 K reservoirs, compute theoretical engine efficiency 40%. For 400 K and 300 K, compute maximum heating COP 4. Contrast this with a device claiming 120% electrical conversion efficiency; explain why the latter is a different claim.
counterexample: Temperatures in Celsius cannot be inserted directly into Carnot ratios. Equal reservoir temperatures create singular ideal COP formulas and no finite-temperature-difference heat engine work.

title: Heat capacity, calorimetry, and phase change
concept: Heating a body requires knowing what its material is, which phase it occupies, and how heat capacity varies with temperature. The approximation Q=mcΔT is useful only where specific heat c is approximately constant and no phase transition occurs. During melting or boiling, latent heat can absorb energy with little temperature change at specified pressure, so a thermometer alone does not measure heat input. Thermochemical databases preserve standard enthalpy, entropy, heat capacities and phase-transition data, but those values depend on pressure, purity and measurement methods. A reconstruction-ready atlas must record source, reference state and uncertainty for every numeric property before using it in an engineering prediction.
formula: Q≈mc_pΔT at constant pressure when c_p is constant; Q_phase=mL; generally Δh=∫c_p(T)dT + phase terms.
derivation: Integrating temperature-dependent heat capacity gives the correct enthalpy change for a single phase under suitable conditions. A simple constant-c calculation is a local approximation to that integral. For a heating curve across a phase boundary, divide the path into sensible-heat and latent-heat intervals. The first law ensures total energy accounting, but the material model determines how input energy changes temperature and phase.
example: Take 1 kg of a hypothetical solid with c=500 J/kg/K, heated by 10 K; compute 5 kJ. Now introduce a phase change with latent heat 50 kJ/kg and explain why adding 50 kJ may not increase temperature.
counterexample: A material property quoted without source, composition, temperature and pressure is not universally valid. Do not extrapolate a heat-capacity table into chemically reactive or high-pressure regimes without evidence.

title: Fourier heat conduction and thermal resistance
concept: Conduction moves heat in response to temperature gradients through a material. Fourier's law links heat flux to thermal conductivity and gradient, with a minus sign indicating flux down temperature. For a one-dimensional uniform slab under steady conditions, the heat rate is kA(Th−Tc)/L. The geometric approximation assumes no internal heat generation, constant conductivity, and negligible multidimensional paths. Thermal resistances in series can be added under the same one-dimensional steady assumption. In real buildings, motor windings and battery packs, contact resistance, radiation, convection and temperature-dependent conductivity matter. A useful calculation must not infer k from a single heat-rate observation without controlling area, thickness and other parallel pathways.
formula: q'' = −k dT/dx; Qdot=kA(Th−Tc)/L; R_thermal=L/(kA).
derivation: Integrate Fourier's law across a slab with constant k and steady uniform flux, giving a linear temperature profile. Resistance form follows by rearrangement. For multiple layers with equal cross-sectional area and series flow, total temperature drop is QdotΣR_i, provided each layer reaches the same steady heat rate. This is a mathematical boundary-value result, not a measurement of a real composite wall.
example: A 0.1 m thick slab has k=1 W/m/K, area 2 m², and 10 K temperature difference. Derive 200 W, then double thickness and compare. Describe how thermal bridging creates departures from 1D predictions.
counterexample: Conductivity units W/(m K) are not the same as heat transfer coefficient W/(m² K). A contact temperature sensor can alter the measured profile and does not certify the model.

title: Convection and convective boundary conditions
concept: Convection combines bulk fluid motion and diffusion near a surface. Newton's cooling relation defines a heat-transfer coefficient h for a chosen geometry and state of fluid motion. This coefficient is not a fundamental constant: it depends on Reynolds number, Prandtl number, orientation, flow regime, fluid properties and characteristic length. Natural and forced convection can differ dramatically. A lumped surface model uses hA(Tsurface−Tfluid), but actual boundary-layer physics may require spatially varying coefficients or computational fluid dynamics. The reference calculation is a bookkeeping tool for a declared h, not an empirical prediction of h from equipment shape.
formula: Qdot_conv=hA(T_surface−T_fluid). Nusselt number Nu=hL/k_fluid, conditional on geometry and flow.
derivation: The heat-transfer coefficient definition rearranges measured heat flux and temperature difference, and empirical correlations may estimate it under limited nondimensional ranges. Choosing an h outside the validity of a correlation can create large error while keeping the equation dimensionally correct. Energy that leaves the surface enters the fluid and must appear in a larger control-volume balance.
example: For h=2 W/m²/K, area=3 m² and a surface 10 K colder than the fluid, the signed convection rate is −60 W using outward-positive convention. Explain the sign and write what an air-speed measurement would need to support an estimated h.
counterexample: A large positive fitted h does not prove high thermal efficiency, and one lab measurement should not be extrapolated to a different Reynolds number or shape.

title: Thermal radiation and the fourth-power law
concept: All bodies above absolute zero exchange electromagnetic radiation. A blackbody has an ideal radiative exitance proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature. Real surfaces have emissivity and wavelength-dependent behavior; geometry introduces view factors, multiple reflections and participating media. A simple net exchange between a gray surface and a large isothermal surrounding environment is epsilon sigma A(T_surface⁴−T_surroundings⁴). That expression is a controlled approximation, not a universal radiative transfer solution. At high temperatures radiation can dominate thermal losses, which makes a linear-temperature approximation unreliable over large differences.
derivation: Stefan–Boltzmann integration of ideal blackbody radiation gives total emitted flux σT⁴. Subtracting an idealized surrounding incident flux gives a net rate. The factor ε is a gray-body approximation; a real spectral emissivity could require integration over wavelength and angles. SI defining constants make the exact derived value of sigma calculable, though the decimal representation is rounded in this code.
example: Calculate the ideal net rate from 400 K to 300 K over one square metre with emissivity one. Reverse temperatures and verify the sign changes but magnitude stays equal. Then explain why changing view factor or emissivity affects a real enclosure.
counterexample: Use kelvin, not degrees Celsius, under a fourth power. A net flux estimate does not prove safe material temperatures or fire resistance.

title: Thermal transients and characteristic time scales
concept: Many real systems do not reach steady state before a measurement or demand change. A lumped thermal model treats a body as spatially isothermal, with thermal capacitance mc and a surface heat transfer hA. Its temperature difference from ambient decays exponentially when no internal heat is generated. The characteristic time is tau=mc/(hA). This model is appropriate only when internal thermal resistance is small relative to boundary heat transfer, commonly assessed with a small Biot number. Battery packs, computing modules, furnace walls and buildings often need spatial models because internal gradients cannot be ignored.
formula: m c dT/dt = −hA(T−T_env); T(t)=T_env+(T0−T_env)e^(−t/τ); τ=mc/(hA).
derivation: Separate variables in the linear first-order differential equation, integrate d(T−Tenv)/(T−Tenv)=−dt/τ, and apply the initial condition. The exponential solution cannot predict sensor response or material changes unless those are modeled. At one time constant the temperature difference is 1/e of its starting value; after several time constants the system approaches ambient asymptotically.
example: For 10 kg, c=500 J/(kg K), h=20 W/(m² K), area=2 m², compute tau=125 s. Compare model temperatures after 125 and 250 s. State what a Biot-number calculation would need before using this on a real motor.
counterexample: A negative or zero time constant is unphysical under this passive model. Uniform temperature and constant h are approximations, not universal physical truths.

title: Electrostatic potential, current, and DC circuits
concept: Electrical work is transferred when charge moves through a potential difference. Current is the rate of charge flow, voltage is energy per unit charge, and resistance models a relationship between current and voltage under specified material conditions. Ohm's law describes ohmic conduction; semiconductor devices, batteries and arcs may be strongly nonlinear. The passive sign convention makes absorbed power p=vi positive when current enters the positive-voltage reference terminal. Sources can deliver electrical power, indicated by negative absorbed power under that convention. Circuit equations enforce charge conservation at nodes and energy balance around loops, but measurement points and grounds must be defined explicitly.
formula: I=dq/dt; V=dW/dq; V=IR for an ohmic element; P=VI; resistive dissipation P=I²R.
derivation: Kirchhoff's current law arises from charge conservation when node charge accumulation is negligible in the chosen circuit representation. Kirchhoff's voltage law relates potential differences around a loop under lumped/quasistatic assumptions. Dividing V by R determines current in a passive linear resistor. Thermal changes can shift R and invalidate a single fixed-resistance prediction.
example: For a 12 V source driving a 6 Ω resistor in an ideal circuit, compute 2 A and 24 W. Integrate over 10 seconds to get 240 J. Explain where the energy goes physically and why a non-ohmic LED should not be treated as a bare resistor.
counterexample: Electricity is dangerous: textbook equations do not specify safe wiring, protection, voltage isolation, fault clearing or operator qualifications. These models must not be used to energize real high-voltage circuits.

title: Capacitors, inductors, and transient storage
concept: Capacitors store energy in electric fields; inductors store energy in magnetic fields. Their constitutive laws connect voltage/current to changes over time. In a simple resistor-capacitor discharge, the voltage falls exponentially with time constant RC. In an inductor, an abrupt current change requires a large induced voltage according to the lumped ideal model, which can cause dangerous switching transients in real equipment. Stored field energy is not the same as delivered energy after conversion losses. Ideal linear component equations neglect parasitic resistance, dielectric absorption, leakage, saturation and breakdown. An engineering energy library must preserve the limitations of a lumped approximation.
formula: E_C=½CV²; E_L=½LI²; i_C=C dv/dt; v_L=L di/dt; V_RC(t)=V0 e^(−t/RC).
derivation: For RC discharge, charge balance gives C dV/dt=−V/R. Separating variables yields exponential voltage and quadratic decay of stored energy. A real capacitor may lose usable energy through series resistance or internal leakage; applying the ideal formula beyond rated voltage can cause component failure. Energy can be conserved while being transformed into resistor heat.
example: A 1 F capacitor at 10 V stores 50 J. Through a 1 Ω resistor, one time constant is 1 second, and the remaining voltage is 10/e V. Derive how much energy has dissipated by that time.
counterexample: An RC time constant is not a battery self-discharge law. Stored energy in a capacitor can be small despite high peak power delivery; never confuse power density and energy density.

title: AC, RMS, power factor, and phasor limits
concept: Alternating current and voltage vary with time. Under sinusoidal steady-state conditions, RMS amplitudes relate to equivalent resistive heating, and phase difference determines real and reactive power. Apparent power is measured in volt-amperes, real power in watts, and reactive power in vars. A power factor of 0.8 means only part of apparent power contributes to average active transfer under the defined sinusoidal model; it does not automatically measure motor mechanical efficiency. Inductive and capacitive loads exchange field energy with the source. Nonsinusoidal waveforms contain harmonics, making simple single-angle formulas insufficient. The direction of reactive power and whether current leads or lags must be declared.
formula: Single-phase sinusoidal: S=V_rms I_rms; P=S cosφ; Q=S sinφ; P²+Q²=S².
derivation: The average of v(t)i(t) over one sinusoidal period gives Vrms Irms cosφ after product-to-sum identities remove a zero-mean double-frequency term. The quadrature component is convention-dependent, so a signed Q requires a stated reactive reference. Three-phase balanced systems sum the three phase powers and simplify to sqrt(3) Vline Iline pf; this fails for arbitrary unbalanced conditions.
example: A 230 V RMS circuit draws 10 A at power factor 0.8. Compute apparent power 2300 VA, real power 1840 W and |reactive| 1380 var. Describe what additional waveforms are needed for a distorted electronic load.
counterexample: Do not use a phase-angle power factor formula to estimate harmonic-rich loads without additional analysis. A high pf is not equivalent to high energy efficiency or improved power-system reliability.

title: Balanced three-phase electricity and transformers
concept: Most bulk electrical systems use three-phase alternating power. Under balanced sinusoidal operation, line voltage and current yield total real power sqrt(3) Vline Iline cosφ. Transformers change voltage and current levels using electromagnetic induction, ideally conserving apparent power while exchanging voltage ratio for current ratio. Real transformers have winding resistance, magnetic core losses, leakage flux, saturation and insulation constraints. Their connection configuration (delta or wye) determines line-to-phase relationships. Voltage step-up can reduce line current for a fixed power transfer and thereby reduce resistive losses, but actual electrical safety, transient stability and grid protection are much more complex than one ideal ratio.
formula: P_3φ=√3 V_LL I_L pf, S_3φ=√3 V_LL I_L; V2/V1≈N2/N1, I1/I2≈N2/N1 (ideal).
derivation: For an ideal transformer, the induced voltage in each winding is proportional to the time derivative of common core flux times its turns; therefore the voltage ratio is the turn ratio. Conservation of instantaneous average power implies the inverse current ratio in magnitude. In a transmission path, I²R scales as current squared, motivating higher voltage for equal transfer. In actual AC networks, conductor resistance, reactive flow, corona effects and stability requirements must also be considered.
example: An ideal 100-turn primary connected to a 200-turn secondary doubles voltage. If the secondary supplies 3 A at 240 V, the primary ideally draws 6 A at 120 V. Recalculate I²R loss for a line with fixed resistance when current is halved.
counterexample: A textbook ideal transformer is not a construction manual or high-voltage clearance procedure. Never energize a real network based on these calculations alone.

title: Electric power grids, losses, and system boundaries
concept: A power grid connects generating resources to loads through transmission, distribution, power electronics, protection devices and control systems. Real grids must balance generation and consumption plus losses at every instant, but frequency and voltage are dynamical states rather than constants guaranteed by an energy sum. A static energy ledger can identify missing accounting but cannot certify angular stability, fault recovery, harmonic limits or protection coordination. High-voltage transmission reduces current for given power and can reduce resistive loss; reactive power and line impedance also matter. A microgrid can operate grid-connected or islanded only when its architecture supports suitable voltage/frequency formation and fault protection. Reliable infrastructure knowledge requires one-line diagrams, equipment nameplates, operating envelopes and tested protection settings, not merely formulas.
formula: Static balance: P_generation + P_import = P_load + P_loss + P_charge + P_export (under defined signs). Line heating P_loss≈I_rms²R for each conductor.
derivation: Kirchhoff's laws enforce network constraints for a lumped electrical model. AC power flow has nonlinear voltage-angle relationships that are not solved by the static scalar balance. Variable renewable generation and storage require time resolution; energy conserved over one day does not guarantee sufficient power at the evening peak. The EIA grid description maps physical stages of generation, transmission and delivery but does not specify one universal real grid.
example: A feeder delivering 10 A through two conductors each of 0.2 Ω loses 40 W in the simple model. Compare with 5 A and hold line resistance constant. Identify which real cable and protection measurements would be necessary before installation.
counterexample: A balanced daily kWh report does not prove every second of demand was met. A standalone grid operation plan needs real-time control and safety validation, outside this reference package.

title: Photovoltaic effects and semiconductor conversion
concept: Photovoltaic cells absorb photons in semiconductor junctions, producing charge carriers that a circuit can collect. Only photons within suitable spectral bands and subject to device losses contribute usefully. A module's rated DC output is measured under standard test conditions, not a guarantee of site power. Array output depends on incident plane-of-array irradiance, cell temperature, spectrum, orientation, shading, soiling, wiring and inverter limits. A useful introductory model scales rated power linearly with irradiance and applies a temperature coefficient around a reference 25°C; it deliberately omits low-light nonlinearities and more detailed diode behavior. Real energy forecasting requires weather series and module characterization.
formula: P_DC≈P_rated(G/1000)(1+γ(T_cell−25°C)) for a specified module, irradiance G in W/m² and gamma in 1/°C.
derivation: Electrical output has dimensions voltage times current. Conversion efficiency is electrical output divided by incident optical power under controlled conditions. The linear model is a first-order expansion of rated module performance around calibration conditions, not a fundamental semiconductor theorem. When a temperature correction becomes negative, the approximation is outside its domain; the reference rejects rather than returning negative generated energy.
example: A rated 1000 W DC array at 1000 W/m² and 45°C with coefficient −0.004/°C produces 920 W under the linear model. Compare the result with measured inverter output and list the components omitted.
counterexample: No perpetual power exists at zero irradiance. A module rating is not a facility capacity factor, and a published record cell efficiency must not be substituted for a installed-array annual yield.

title: Wind turbines, aerodynamic power, and Betz’s ideal limit
concept: The kinetic energy flux through a rotor-swept area is proportional to density, area and the cube of wind speed. A turbine can extract only part of that flux; the ideal steady actuator-disk model gives the Betz maximum power coefficient 16/27. Real machines also obey cut-in, rated, cut-out and fatigue limits. Wind fields vary with height, terrain, atmospheric stability and turbulence. Power curves measured at standard conditions cannot simply be multiplied by a regional average wind speed; because power scales with the cube of speed before rating, the distribution matters. A full resource assessment needs hub-height wind time series, air density, array losses and electrical conversion data.
formula: P_wind=½ρAv³; P_rotor=CpP_wind, 0≤Cp≤16/27 in the ideal actuator-disk model.
derivation: For a mass flow of air moving at velocity v, kinetic energy per mass is v²/2 and volume flow scales with Av, giving kinetic power ρAv³/2. Betz's result balances upstream and downstream momentum across a slowed ideal stream tube; extracting all energy would halt the flow and eliminate throughput. The upper bound does not apply to arbitrary non-actuator devices or justify real turbine efficiency measurements.
example: For air density 1.2 kg/m³, area 10 m², speed 10 m/s and Cp=0.4, compute 2400 W. Double wind speed and explain the eightfold ideal pre-rated power increase. Then explain why a real turbine would reach rated power and eventually shut down.
counterexample: A power coefficient above 16/27 should trigger model review, not be reported as evidence of revolutionary wind physics. Real coefficients and measurement boundaries must be distinguished.

title: Hydropower, head, and water resources
concept: Water moving through a height difference can transfer gravitational potential energy to a turbine. Under a simple incompressible steady model, available power scales with density, gravitational acceleration, volumetric flow and head. Turbine-generator efficiency converts hydraulic head into electric output. Real systems have penstock friction, changing reservoir levels, cavitation risk, environmental flow constraints, sediment and regulatory requirements. Pumped storage uses electricity to move water uphill and later recover some energy; it is storage with losses, not a source that creates energy. River hydrology and site surveys matter more than assuming one permanent head and flow.
formula: P_hydro=ρgQHη; hydraulic power P_available=ρgQH, 0≤η≤1.
derivation: Potential energy of mass m at elevation difference H is mgH; mass flow rate is ρQ, yielding power ρgQH. Efficiency accounts for mechanical and electrical conversion within a declared boundary. The formula does not provide environmental suitability or legal authority to alter waterways. Scaling flow in a hypothetical example is simple; predicting real available flow across seasons is not.
example: With water density 1000 kg/m³, flow 1 m³/s, net head 10 m and conversion efficiency 0.8, calculate approximately 78.5 kW. Halve flow and compare, while listing the flow and head surveys a real project would require.
counterexample: Head and flow cannot be assumed constant from a single measurement. A physically feasible power calculation is not a permit, safety assessment or ecological-impact study.

title: Geothermal heat and direct thermal services
concept: Geothermal resources exploit thermal energy in Earth's subsurface. Applications include direct heat, district heating, ground-source heat pumps and geothermal electricity where temperature and flow are sufficient. Ground-source heat pumps do not usually tap deep high-temperature geothermal reservoirs; they use the ground as a moderate-temperature exchange environment. Resource adequacy depends on permeability, temperature gradient, sustainable heat extraction, fluid chemistry and drilling conditions. A simplified thermal power estimate requires mass flow and enthalpy difference, not merely underground temperature. Resource classifications, induced seismicity and water chemistry are distinct from thermodynamic possibility.
formula: P_thermal≈ṁ(h_in−h_out), with mass flow ṁ in kg/s and specific enthalpy h in J/kg.
derivation: The steady-flow first law accounts for enthalpy transported by the working fluid, plus pumps, heat exchange and mechanical work. For pure liquid under narrow temperature range h change may be approximated with c_pΔT. The approximation breaks down across phase changes and significant pressure effects. A real electricity cycle needs a heat sink and faces Carnot/exergy constraints.
example: Construct a stream of 1 kg/s cooling through 20 K with constant c_p=4200 J/kg/K, giving 84 kW of thermal transfer. Specify why this cannot be interpreted as 84 kW of electrical output without a thermodynamic cycle and temperature bounds.
counterexample: Geothermal heat is not globally uniform or always indefinitely renewable at a particular extraction rate. Source temperature alone cannot establish project viability.

title: Heat engines, Rankine cycles, and combined heat and power
concept: Thermal power plants convert some heat from combustion, fission, concentrated solar or geothermal processes into mechanical and then electrical work. Real cycles use pumps, turbines, heat exchangers and condensers. The Rankine cycle is a foundational steam-power model; Brayton cycles underpin gas turbines. Cogeneration or combined heat and power (CHP) captures thermal output for useful heating or industrial service, improving total useful-energy utilization without violating heat-engine efficiency limits. Plant efficiency depends on fuel higher or lower heating value, ambient conditions, equipment condition, load and heat-demand matching. Condenser rejection and cooling infrastructure are part of the energy balance.
formula: η_electric = W_electric/Q_fuel; η_CHP_useful=(W_electric+Q_useful_heat)/Q_fuel; 0≤η≤1 within closed fuel-energy boundary.
derivation: For a heat engine, first-law balance partitions heat input into work and rejected heat over a complete cycle. CHP counts only heat that actually serves a validated demand; dumping unwanted low-grade heat does not increase useful efficiency. A plant reporting higher electrical efficiency may still have different fuel boundaries and lower heating value reference. Second-law analysis constrains feasible temperature-limited work extraction.
example: A plant consumes 100 units of fuel energy and produces 30 units electric work, 40 units useful heat, and 30 units other rejection. Calculate electrical efficiency 30% and combined useful efficiency 70%, then identify the necessary heat-customer operating schedule.
counterexample: Do not add thermal energy at one temperature to electricity as if both had identical usefulness in exergy or economic value. A CHP figure cannot exceed the physically accounted fuel input without investigating omitted energy sources.

title: Nuclear binding energy and controlled fission electricity
concept: Nuclear reactions convert differences in nuclear binding energy into kinetic energy and radiation, much of which becomes heat in reactor systems. The mass-energy relation E=Δmc² describes an ideal mass defect, not a complete prediction of a plant's electric output. Commercial fission plants use controlled chain reactions, heat removal, steam cycles, shielding and multiple safety systems. Distinguish the microscopic energy of fission events from reactor thermal power, turbine mechanical output, generator efficiency, operating capacity factor and waste-management requirements. The scientific reference can teach energy conservation and mass defect without offering design or operational instructions for radioactive materials or reactors.
formula: E_released≈Δm c²; c=299792458 m/s (exact), with mass defect Δm in kg.
derivation: A reaction's initial and final rest masses differ; conservation of mass-energy means released energy appears as motion, photons or other channels. Simply multiplying a bulk mass by c² is not a claim that all that matter can be converted in a practical reactor. Fuel composition, reaction pathways, thermal conversion efficiency, capacity limits and safety constraints make actual electricity generation far smaller than naïve all-mass conversion examples.
example: For a hypothetical mass difference of 10^-9 kg, compute approximately 8.99×10^7 J. Explicitly state that this is an algebraic conversion of a *specified* mass defect, not a fuel recipe, reactor yield or measurement.
counterexample: Do not use this reference to assemble, operate or modify a nuclear system. The absence of operational instructions is intentional, and reactor safety requires qualified regulatory engineering.

title: Fusion physics and unverified commercial performance
concept: Fusion joins light nuclei into heavier products and can release binding energy under particular reaction conditions. Stars sustain fusion through extreme temperatures and gravitational confinement. Terrestrial research explores plasma confinement, turbulence, plasma-facing materials, sustained burning, tritium fuel cycles and engineering conversion of heat to electricity. A reported scientific fusion gain can use a narrow accounting boundary (for example energy delivered to a target versus fusion output), while a commercial plant must account for all facility energy input, heat conversion, recirculating power, reliability and maintenance. The distinction is essential for honest claims. The current scientific literature and DOE programs describe active progress but do not imply that every proposed architecture has demonstrated grid-scale economic electricity.
formula: Q_plasma=E_fusion/E_auxiliary_heating under a declared plasma boundary; overall electric efficiency requires facility net electrical output/input accounting.
derivation: Reaction mass defects follow E=Δmc²; achieving a net facility gain depends on confinement, material integrity, fuel supply and conversion. One ratio cannot substitute for another when denominators differ. An energy balance across a larger boundary may reveal laser, cryogenic, magnet or support-power costs excluded from a small-boundary Q. This is not a critique of a specific experiment without its original measurements; it is a general accounting requirement.
example: Given a toy plasma experiment with 10 arbitrary units of fusion output and 5 units of plasma heating, report Q_plasma=2, then add 20 units of facility overhead and show why the facility has not demonstrated positive net electrical output in that toy scenario.
counterexample: Never equate plasma gain, wall-plug gain and net delivered electricity. Fusion fuel cycles, materials and regulatory constraints remain experimental and engineering questions.

title: Electrochemical batteries and capacity versus power
concept: Rechargeable batteries store energy through chemical potentials and convert between electrical and chemical energy through electrochemical reactions. Their nominal capacity is often quoted in ampere-hours or watt-hours, but usable capacity depends on voltage, temperature, discharge rate, age, cell balance and allowed state-of-charge limits. Power capability depends on internal resistance, electrode kinetics, thermal management and protection electronics. A battery with high energy capacity need not provide high short-duration power, and a high-power cell need not provide large total energy. Battery management systems protect cells against overcharge, deep discharge, overcurrent and thermal events; a formula for state of charge is not a substitute for such protection.
formula: E_stored≈∫V_terminal I dt within stated sign convention; nominal energy ≈ V_nominal×Ah, not exact if voltage varies.
derivation: Chemical free-energy differences drive an open-circuit cell potential, while terminal voltage differs under load because of internal losses and polarization. Coulomb counting integrates current but accumulates measurement bias and must be corrected by calibration or independent state estimates. A pack has cell-level safety limits that can bind before the nominal overall energy is exhausted.
example: A nominal 10 V, 100 Ah storage unit is often labeled 1 kWh. Explain why measuring terminal voltage under a varying load is necessary for a better energy estimate, and why 1 kWh capacity does not guarantee that a 2 kW load can be supplied for 30 minutes safely.
counterexample: Do not use a simple energy-balance model as battery charging firmware or a safety controller. Chemistry-dependent thermal runaway risks, degradation and BMS limits require separate validated engineering.

title: Battery charging, round-trip losses, and state of charge
concept: A useful elementary battery model tracks stored energy in kWh, charge input and delivered discharge power. With fixed one-way efficiencies, stored energy increases by η_charge P_charge Δt and decreases by P_discharge Δt/η_discharge. The difference appears as loss and heat under a chosen accounting boundary. A round trip through the battery returns less electrical energy than supplied unless idealized efficiencies equal one. This says nothing about Coulombic efficiency, calendar aging, nonlinear voltage, cell mismatch or safe charge acceptance. A physically accountable model rejects a step that exceeds capacity rather than silently clipping storage and hiding the excess energy.
formula: E_next=E_current+η_ch P_ch Δt−P_dis Δt/η_dis; η_roundtrip≈η_chη_dis (matched boundaries).
derivation: The relation follows from ordinary energy accounting: input electrical energy times charge efficiency becomes stored chemical energy, while delivered electrical energy requires a larger internal energy decrease. Defining the reference endpoints matters: including inverter and transformer losses changes efficiency. In a multi-hour dispatch the battery's power rating, state-dependent performance and reserve constraints must be modeled in addition to energy capacity.
example: Start with 5 kWh in a 10 kWh idealized battery. Charge at 2 kW for one hour with η_ch=.9, obtaining 6.8 kWh. Then discharge a specified amount and compute how much internally stored energy must be consumed at η_dis=.8.
counterexample: A step that requests more than available energy is invalid. Automatically changing output without explicitly recording curtailed discharge invents a delivered service that was never supplied.

title: Hydrogen and electrochemical conversion pathways
concept: Hydrogen is an energy carrier produced from other primary energy sources. Electrolysis uses electrical work to split water, while fuel cells can convert chemical reaction free energy into electrical work. Hydrogen production efficiency must specify lower or higher heating value, water conditions and whether heat inputs are included. Storage and transport require compression, liquefaction or other engineering approaches that consume energy and introduce losses. A hydrogen production pathway can be useful for specific industrial feedstocks or storage use cases, but hydrogen conversion is not a net energy source: the energy delivered from a complete production-storage-conversion chain cannot exceed all energy entering its boundary.
formula: E_electrical_in=E_chemical_H2/η_electrolysis under one declared heating-value convention; E_electric_out≈η_fuelcell E_chemical_H2.
derivation: The complete system efficiency is the product of sequential efficiencies under consistent accounting conventions. Changing from LHV to HHV shifts numeric reported percentages without altering physical energy, so reference basis must be stated. Faraday's law connects charge passed to a theoretical amount of electrochemical product, but actual Faradaic efficiency and gas purity require measurements. Real safety includes flammable gas handling, pressure vessels and leak detection.
example: Assume synthetic stage efficiencies .7 for electrolyzer, .9 for storage/transport and .5 for fuel cell. Multiply to get .315 overall energy efficiency, then explain why the result is not a forecast of any specific technology's economics.
counterexample: Do not infer water splitting is over-unity because a fuel cell later returns electricity. Hydrogen storage and gas-handling design require accredited safety practice, absent here.

title: Thermal, gravitational, mechanical, and pumped storage
concept: Electricity can be stored indirectly as gravitational potential, kinetic energy, compressed fluid, phase-change heat or chemical energy. Each mechanism has a different energy density, response time, efficiency, site requirement and durability. Pumped hydro returns water downhill after using electricity to pump it upward, with a round-trip loss. Flywheel energy grows with the square of angular speed, but mechanical stress and containment impose limits. Sensible thermal storage uses heat capacity; phase-change storage adds latent heat at appropriate temperatures. Compressed-air storage interacts with thermodynamics of compression and expansion, so a pressure-only calculation is inadequate. Selecting a technology requires a service definition: seconds of fast response, days of shifting, industrial process heat or seasonal energy supply.
formula: E_gravity=mgh; E_flywheel=½Iω²; E_sensible≈mcΔT; round-trip η=E_delivered/E_supplied under matched interfaces.
derivation: Each expression follows from a work integral under a specified physical model: gravitational work over height, rotational kinetic energy from torque and angular acceleration, and heat capacity from enthalpy change. A real storage system includes friction, converter losses, heat leaks and hardware limits. Stored energy is not automatically recoverable as electricity at a given rated power.
example: For a mass of 1000 kg raised 10 m, compute gravitational storage as 98.1 kJ. Compare with 1 kWh and state why a practical pumped-storage facility requires substantial water flow, head and turbine/generator systems.
counterexample: Never interpret mechanical storage formulas as instructions to construct high-speed rotors or pressurized vessels. Safe containment, fatigue and fault analysis are specialized fields.

title: Power rating, energy capacity, and capacity factor
concept: Power capacity states an instantaneous or sustained rate, while energy capacity states how much service can be delivered over time. A 100 kW generator at 50% capacity factor produces half the energy it would produce at continuous full rating over the defined interval, but capacity factor does not equal thermodynamic efficiency. A battery rated at 100 kW and 100 kWh has a nominal one-hour duration at rated power under ideal conversion, yet usable duration depends on efficiency, allowable discharge and temperature. Capacity factors for intermittent sources must be computed over actual hourly generation, not from one favorable period. Outages, dispatch restrictions and curtailment are distinct contributors to lower output.
formula: Capacity factor CF=E_generated/(P_rated×Δt), 0≤CF≤1 for physical output under the same rating and interval.
derivation: The denominator is the hypothetical upper-bound energy if the plant produced nameplate power throughout the period. Actual output integrates instantaneous power. CF is a utilization measure; it does not describe fuel conversion efficiency or operating margins. Comparing technologies requires equivalent measured boundaries and service value, not merely ranking CF.
example: A 100 kW resource delivers 500 kWh during a ten-hour period, so CF=.5. Calculate the same resource's CF if output was curtailed by 100 kWh, and identify whether physical resource, demand or reliability explains the change.
counterexample: A reported CF above one signals inconsistent rated capacity, measurement scope, time interval or data, rather than a breakthrough in energy conversion.

title: Distributed generation, storage dispatch, and unmet load
concept: A small isolated electrical system must provide sufficient instantaneous power while respecting storage power and energy constraints. A dispatch model consumes timeseries of renewable generation and load, routes surplus into charging where available, and records curtailed generation or imported energy separately. During deficits it discharges storage within limits, then records unmet demand or required grid imports. A daily kWh balance alone cannot guarantee power adequacy at a specific time. Storage dispatch may require forecast uncertainty, reserve policies and reactive power support that a scalar energy model does not provide. A valid ledger must distinguish load actually served from demand requested and must not silently create energy by clipping battery state.
formula: For each interval: generation + discharge + import = served_load + charge + export + curtailment + losses, with all terms sign-consistent.
derivation: The interval balance follows from conservation. A battery step adds state continuity between intervals. If maximum charge and discharge powers are not imposed, a model can make impossible spikes even with adequate total kWh. If reserve and grid-forming requirements are omitted, the result is only an idealized energy feasibility exercise. Matching all energy flows is necessary but insufficient for voltage and frequency stability.
example: Construct a two-hour toy load series 1 kW then 3 kW, with solar 3 kW then 0 and a 2 kWh battery. Allocate surplus and deficit, record charge/discharge losses, and identify any unmet load with no grid connection. Use separate source and storage states.
counterexample: Do not claim a functioning or safe microgrid from an energy-only simulation. A grid needs protection, frequency regulation, grounding and synchronized power-electronic controls.

title: Renewable variability, curtailment, and temporal matching
concept: Wind and solar output vary with weather, time and geographic conditions. An average capacity factor cannot reveal whether generation meets load at the right hours. Time correlation between supply and demand, storage duration, interconnection limits and reserve requirements determine reliability. Curtailment means available renewable output is not used because of grid constraints, market signals or equipment conditions; it is not evidence the sunlight or wind contained no energy. A strong analytical library preserves time-series provenance, sampling rate, missing intervals, calendar/time zones, asset rating and measurement uncertainty. Aggregating all hours into one annual energy total can conceal damaging outages.
formula: Net load(t)=Load(t)−VariableGeneration(t); E_deficit=∫max(0,NetLoad(t))dt under a declared time series and no storage.
derivation: The max operator separates deficit periods from surplus. Integrating the signed net load can cancel surpluses and deficits that occur at different times, implying false instantaneous feasibility. Storage can shift some energy but incurs losses, finite duration and finite power. Different weather years can lead to different adequacy outcomes even if annual mean production is similar.
example: Compare two synthetic hours: renewable output 4 kW then 0, load 2 kW each hour. Total generation equals total demand, but without storage the second hour has 2 kWh unmet. Explain the role of a battery and why a 2 kWh nameplate may not suffice with efficiency losses.
counterexample: Do not equate annual net-zero energy with continuous reliability or zero environmental impact. The problem is temporal and spatial matching.

title: Energy economics, discounted cost, and LCOE
concept: Levelized cost of energy compares discounted lifecycle cost to discounted energy output under a specified project model. It can be useful for alternatives but does not by itself value when electricity is available, how reliably it meets peak demand, local grid constraints or the external impacts of a project. Capital cost, financing, capacity factor, fuel, maintenance, decommissioning, salvage and policy can change results. Real and nominal discount rates must not be mixed with inflation assumptions. A single cost figure cannot represent affordability for every community or determine technology desirability without service and risk analysis.
formula: LCOE=(C0+Σ_t C_t/(1+r)^t)/(Σ_t E_t/(1+r)^t), in currency/kWh if E in kWh and currency units consistent.
derivation: Discounting expresses time preference and financing assumptions by placing future costs and output on a common present-value basis. The formula is an accounting ratio, not a physical law. If production is zero the denominator vanishes, making a numeric cost per kWh undefined. A model that reports LCOE without the generation series, assumptions and full time horizon is not reconstructible.
example: Choose illustrative capital cost 1000 units and ten years of 100 units annual cost and 1000 kWh output, with discount .05. Recompute using the reference code and then reduce generation 30% to see the increase. Do not present synthetic currency units as market prices.
counterexample: A lower LCOE does not automatically mean lower total system cost. Firm capacity, grid reinforcement, reliability and external impacts are outside this simple formula.

title: Energy in computation and physical information processing
concept: Computers consume electricity and dissipate heat while performing information processing. The energy used per operation depends on architecture, memory access, switching activity, voltage, clock rate, data movement, cooling and utilization. A count of model tokens, bit operations or agent steps is not by itself joules consumed. Dynamic CMOS power is approximately proportional to switching capacitance, voltage squared and frequency, subject to technology and workload. Memory bandwidth and cooling can dominate arithmetic energy. Energy efficiency comparisons require equal quality targets, measured power over a full interval and consideration of idle baseline. A routing system that reduces apparent model calls may still increase total energy by performing more memory retrieval or verification.
formula: P_dynamic≈αCV²f; E_compute=∫P_wall(t)dt; energy per successful task = E_total/N_verified_successes.
derivation: Charging/discharging capacitive nodes gives the voltage-squared dynamic-power dependence, with activity factor absorbing average switching. This is a schematic physical model, not a calibrated description of a modern CPU or GPU. To evaluate an AI system, measure wall power and task outcome under identical conditions, including CPU/GPU, network and storage contributions. A reduction in latency is not necessarily energy reduction if active power rises.
example: Measure or hypothesize a 100 W computing system running for 30 seconds: 3000 J. If 10 tasks ran but only 5 were independently verified successful, energy per successful task is 600 J under the measured boundary. Explain how idle power changes that comparison.
counterexample: No Bitwork energy-saving advantage can be established from a frequency-only synthetic benchmark or from token counts without actual hardware measurements at controlled task quality.

title: Energy measurements, uncertainty, and calibration
concept: A scientific energy measurement begins by defining the measurand: electrical energy delivered to a load, chemical energy content of fuel, net heat transfer, or whole-facility electricity. Instruments have calibration uncertainty, resolution, drift, bandwidth, phase error and sampling limits. Measuring voltage and current separately does not always recover instantaneous real power, particularly with phase shift or distorted waveforms; a proper power analyzer integrates their product with synchronized sampling. Measurement uncertainties can be correlated, making simple independent-root-sum-of-squares formulas inadequate. A reconstructible result preserves device, calibration record, measurement interval, reference conditions and uncertainty propagation.
formula: E≈Σ_i (P_i+P_(i+1))/2 × Δt_i for trapezoidal interpolation; u_y²≈Σ_i(∂f/∂x_i)²u_i² plus covariance terms.
derivation: Trapezoidal integration is exact for linear power variation between samples, but real transients between measurement points can be missed. Error propagation follows first-order linearization of the measurement model around estimates; it is not automatically valid for large nonlinear or non-Gaussian uncertainty. A robust study includes a second measurement method or known calibration source where possible.
example: Integrate three synthetic samples (t=0,10,20 s; P=10,10,20 W), giving 250 J by trapezoidal rule. Describe a pulse between samples that this calculation would completely miss. State an appropriate sampling or anti-aliasing plan.
counterexample: A numerical result with many decimal places does not prove high physical accuracy. Calibration and timing traceability determine the defensible significant figures.

title: Efficiency versus exergy versus capacity factor
concept: Energy conversion efficiency, thermodynamic exergetic efficiency, round-trip storage efficiency and generator capacity factor answer different questions. An electric motor can have high conversion efficiency while running only a few hours; its capacity utilization is then low. A heat pump can have COP greater than one while obeying the first and second laws. A thermal engine is bounded by the temperature of its heat source and sink. A perfect first-law balance can still have enormous exergy destruction through mixing or friction. A robust comparison must preserve each metric's numerator, denominator, source boundary, time interval and quality of output.
formula: η_converter=E_useful/E_in≤1 under ordinary conversion; COP_heating=Q_delivered/W_input; CF=E_generated/(P_rated Δt).
derivation: The distinctions arise from different accounting denominators. A heat pump counts thermal energy moved from the environment as useful delivery, unlike a passive conversion ratio. A capacity factor compares delivered energy against rated full-power potential over time. An exergetic metric estimates useful work potential relative to environment. Conflating the metrics creates false over-unity headlines or misleading technology rankings.
example: Compare a 70%-efficient conversion device, a heat pump with COP 3, and a generator with CF .3. Describe what the number means in each case and why there is no simple universal ordering of energy performance.
counterexample: A device efficiency greater than 100% is suspicious only after its precise definition is identified. Claims of net energy creation remain inconsistent with conservation unless unreported inputs or boundaries resolve the discrepancy.

title: Lifecycle impacts, carbon accounting, and resource constraints
concept: Energy technologies have impacts across materials extraction, fabrication, construction, operation, fuel supply, maintenance and end of life. Direct plant-stack emissions are not the same as lifecycle greenhouse-gas intensity. A battery or solar panel may have zero direct combustion emissions during operation but embodied manufacturing impacts, land/water demand and recycling constraints. Assessments must state functional unit such as grams CO2-equivalent per delivered kWh, system boundary, grid mix, recycling allocation and time horizon. Numeric environmental comparisons should come from harmonized datasets, not invented generic constants. Economic and climate objectives can conflict with local ecological or social constraints.
formula: I_lifecycle=(Σ stage emissions_kgCO2e)/(Σ life delivered kWh), under documented boundary and attribution method.
derivation: The ratio is an inventory quotient, not a universal physical property of a technology. Its denominator can vary with device life, degradation, climate and curtailment; the numerator can vary with the electricity mix used in manufacture and accounting conventions. Independent lifecycle evidence requires audited upstream inputs and sensitivity analysis. An energy-only model cannot validate greenhouse-gas emissions or social effects.
example: Use a constructed device with 1000 kgCO2e embodied impact and 10000 kWh lifetime delivery, yielding 0.1 kgCO2e/kWh. Halve its lifetime production and demonstrate that intensity doubles. Explain why this example is not a measured technology result.
counterexample: Do not assign a zero lifecycle impact to a zero-stack-emission resource, or confuse different CO2-equivalence time horizons and allocation rules.

title: Resilient power: microgrids, islanding, and critical loads
concept: Power resilience means preserving essential services despite disruptions. A robust microgrid must identify critical loads, generator and storage operating constraints, fault detection, protection, grid-forming controls, communications, fuel supplies and trained operators. The sequence of safe islanding and reconnection is specific to equipment and utility interconnection rules. A simplified energy budget can estimate whether a hospital's nominal battery stores enough kWh, but cannot guarantee safe operation under high inrush currents, reactive loads, faults or equipment failure. Recovery priorities also depend on human needs, not just objective functions. A survival atlas should teach the distinction between energy planning and legally authorized electrical operations.
formula: Critical-load energy minimum E_need≈∫P_critical(t)dt; storage usable delivery < nameplate capacity after SOC reserve and conversion losses.
derivation: The expression integrates demand, but a real plan must check peak kW, power quality, switching and fault capability. Resilience also requires scenario analysis: cloudy periods, fuel interruption, battery faults and communication loss can be correlated. A design that meets average load may still fail an emergency peak. Service restoration must be supervised by qualified professionals with tested emergency procedures.
example: Construct an emergency schedule with one 500 W critical load for 8 hours: 4 kWh before storage losses. Compare to a nominal 5 kWh battery at 80% usable depth of discharge and 90% discharge efficiency, giving only 3.6 kWh delivered; identify the deficit.
counterexample: Do not energize emergency electrical equipment or attempt grid islanding from this manual. Protective coordination, certification and qualified engineering are essential.

title: Reconstruction of energy systems after infrastructure loss
concept: Preserving energy knowledge for future generations requires more than an encyclopedia of device names. The library should make it possible to trace a physical service—light, heating, refrigeration, pumping or communications—from energy resource to useful demand through conversion and control. A future reader needs original principles, material properties with source and temperature, calibrated measurement practices, construction standards and safety limitations. It is important to preserve what is not included: this research version cannot safely instruct a nonexpert to build a high-voltage substation, pressure plant or nuclear reactor. Rebuilding technical civilization demands trained people, supply chains and verified standards as well as equations.
formula: Reconstruction chain: resource → conversion → transmission/storage → controlled load → independently measured service, with signed energy ledger at each stage.
derivation: A system-of-systems argument requires every interface to preserve units, time basis and conservation. The receiving system's efficiency and operating envelope depend on upstream outputs and downstream loads. For example, a solar array, inverter and battery may each have a valid small-model equation, but combining them safely requires live protection and power-control specifications not represented in this corpus. Complete method reconstruction includes installation constraints, maintenance, calibration and failure diagnosis, and each missing piece should be named.
example: Start with the goal of powering a 10 W communications radio for 24 hours. Compute 240 Wh ideal load, then add a declared converter loss and storage reserve. Explain why the energy estimate does not certify antenna operation, battery safety, or power quality.
counterexample: The term “humanity's last knowledge” is an acceptance aspiration. Energy Atlas v0.1 is not a complete primary-source archive, qualified engineering specification or substitute for safety expertise.
